2020: Jeremiah, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a). The book cites earlier written sources: the Book of the Acts of Solomon (1 Kgs 11:41) and the chronicles of the kings of Israel and of Judah.
2021: The central part of the Deuteronomistic History. Major models include Noth's single exilic author, Frank Moore Cross's two editions (a Josianic edition celebrating Josiah, updated in exile), and the Göttingen school's several exilic layers (historical, prophetic and nomistic). Most agree it drew on royal annals and prophetic story collections.
2023: Traditional view: compiled by Jeremiah in exile
2024: Israelites in or after the exile asking why the kingdom divided and fell, read in light of the covenant demands of Deuteronomy.
2025: From David's death and Solomon's accession (c. 970 BC) through the divided kingdoms to the death of Ahab of Israel and the reign of Jehoshaphat of Judah (mid 9th century BC).
2026: To evaluate each king by loyalty to the LORD and to worship at the Jerusalem temple, to show prophets as God's covenant enforcers, and to explain how idolatry led to division and decline.
2029: Division of the kingdom as judgment
2030: The prophetic word fulfilled in history
2039: Kings of Judah and Israel to Ahab
2041: Drought and the widow of Zarephath
2044: Naboth's vineyard; Micaiah and Ahab's death
2045: 1 Kings shows the high point of Israel's monarchy in Solomon's temple and its swift unravelling through idolatry, setting up the long road to exile. Jesus points to himself as 'greater than Solomon' (Matt 12:42) and the true temple, and Elijah reappears in the expectation of a returning prophet fulfilled, in the Gospels' view, in John the Baptist.
2046: 1 and 2 Kings form one book in the Hebrew Bible and close the Former Prophets. The Septuagint calls them 3 and 4 Kingdoms and has significant differences of order and content in the Solomon and Jeroboam chapters.
2048: Jeremiah, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), with the final chapter possibly added by a later hand; 2 Kgs 24:18-25:30 closely matches Jer 52.
2049: The conclusion of the Deuteronomistic History. On Cross's double-redaction model, a first edition climaxed with Josiah's reform (2 Kgs 22-23) and an exilic editor added the fall of Jerusalem; Noth argued for a single exilic author; the Göttingen school sees multiple exilic layers. The last event recorded, the release of Jehoiachin by Evil-merodach (c. 561 BC), sets the earliest date for the final form.
2050: Judeans in Babylonian exile, needing to understand why Israel and Judah fell and whether any hope remained for David's line.
2051: From the mid 9th century (Ahaziah of Israel, Elisha's ministry) through the fall of Samaria to Assyria (722 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon (586 BC) and the exile.
2052: To justify God's judgment by showing persistent covenant unfaithfulness despite repeated prophetic warnings, to honour reforming kings like Hezekiah and Josiah, and to leave a flicker of hope in the release of David's heir.
2053: The power of the prophetic word (Elijah and Elisha)
2063: Israel and Judah to the fall of Samaria
2066: Later kings of Israel and Judah
2067: Fall of Samaria and its explanation
2073: 2 Kings ends the story of the monarchy in ruins, with temple burned and people exiled, raising the question the prophets answer: will God keep his promise to David? Jesus cites Elisha's healing of the foreigner Naaman (Luke 4:27), and the hope left open by Jehoiachin's release is carried forward in the genealogy that runs through him to Jesus (Matt 1:11-12).
2074: Second half of the single Hebrew book of Kings (Former Prophets); '4 Kingdoms' in the Septuagint. Parallel accounts appear in 2 Chronicles, Isa 36-39 and Jer 52.
2076: Historical narrative with genealogies (theological retelling of Israel's history)
2077: Ezra, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a). The overlap between the end of 2 Chronicles and the start of Ezra (2 Chr 36:22-23; Ezra 1:1-3) was long taken as evidence of one author.
2078: An anonymous writer usually called 'the Chronicler', probably a Levite or someone close to temple circles in Persian-period Jerusalem. Older scholarship assumed common authorship with Ezra–Nehemiah; since the work of Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson (1960s–70s) many scholars treat them as separate works because of differences in language and outlook. The Chronicler used Samuel–Kings as a main source, plus other sources it names.
2079: Earlier Persian period, soon after the temple's rebuilding
2082: The restored community in Judah after the exile, small and under Persian rule, needing to know that they were still 'all Israel', heirs of David's promise and the temple's worship.
2083: Written in Persian-period Judah; the narrative runs from Adam (in genealogy) to the death of David, focusing on David's reign and preparations for the temple.
2084: To retell Israel's story for the post-exilic community, stressing continuity with the past, the centrality of temple worship and Levitical service, and the Davidic promise as grounds for hope.
2086: David as founder of temple worship
2087: Levites, priests and music in worship
2088: Seeking the LORD and immediate retribution or blessing
2089: Continuity from Adam to the restored community
2090: Genealogies from Adam to the returned exiles
2092: The tribes, with Judah and Levi prominent
2093: Inhabitants of Jerusalem after the exile
2096: David made king; his mighty men
2097: The ark brought to Jerusalem; thanksgiving psalm
2099: Preparations and organisation for the temple
2100: Charge to Solomon; David's prayer and death
2101: Chronicles retells the whole Old Testament story in compressed form for people living after the exile, insisting that God's promise to David and his presence in worship still define Israel. Matthew's genealogy, beginning with 'the son of David, the son of Abraham' (Matt 1:1), echoes the Chronicler's way of telling history through family lines.
2102: 1 and 2 Chronicles are one book in the Hebrew Bible, usually the last book of the Writings, so the Hebrew Bible closes with Cyrus' call to go up to Jerusalem. The Septuagint called it *Paralipomena* ('things left out'), as if a supplement to Samuel–Kings; Jerome suggested the title 'chronicle' of the whole sacred history.
2104: Historical narrative (theological retelling of the history of Judah)
2105: Ezra, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a).
2106: The same anonymous Chronicler as 1 Chronicles, probably a Levite in Persian-period Jerusalem. The writer reworks Kings, omitting most material about the northern kingdom, and cites other prophetic and royal records. Scholars debate how much the non-Kings material reflects lost sources and how much is the Chronicler's theological shaping.
2108: The post-exilic community in Judah, encouraged to seek the LORD, honour the temple and trust that repentance brings restoration.
2109: From Solomon's accession (c. 970 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC), ending with Cyrus' decree permitting return (538 BC).
2110: To show that Judah's fortunes rose and fell with its faithfulness to the LORD and the temple, to model repentance and reform, and to end with the open door of return under Cyrus.
2111: The temple as the centre of national life
2112: Seeking the LORD and humbling oneself
2113: Immediate consequences of faithfulness and unfaithfulness
2114: Reform under good kings (Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah)
2115: Repentance and restoration even for the worst (Manasseh)
2120: Kings of Judah from Rehoboam to Ahaz
2124: From Hezekiah to the exile and return
2127: Fall of Jerusalem and Cyrus' decree
2128: 2 Chronicles closes the Hebrew Bible with exile and an invitation to return, leaving Israel waiting for full restoration under a son of David. Its focus on the temple as the place where God's glory dwells prepares for the New Testament claim that this presence is found in Jesus and his people.
2129: The *Prayer of Manasseh*, a short penitential prayer based on 2 Chr 33:12-13 and 2 Chr 33:18-19, is canonical in Eastern Orthodox Bibles (among the Odes), appears in an appendix to the Latin Vulgate, and was included among the Apocrypha in Protestant Bibles such as the 1611 King James Version. It is not part of the Catholic deuterocanon.
2131: Historical narrative with lists, official documents and first-person memoir
2132: Ezra the priest and scribe, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), who is also credited there with Chronicles. Parts of the book are written in the first person by Ezra (Ezra 7:27-9:15).
2133: An anonymous editor compiled Ezra–Nehemiah from sources: an Ezra memoir, lists of returnees, and Aramaic documents from the Persian court (Ezra 4:8-6:18; Ezra 7:12-26). Scholars debate the authenticity of these documents (many accept that they reflect genuine Persian administrative style) and the order of Ezra and Nehemiah: the text places Ezra first (458 BC, the seventh year of Artaxerxes I), but some argue for Artaxerxes II (398 BC), which would place Ezra after Nehemiah.
2135: Ezra's arrival dated to Artaxerxes II
2137: Jews in Judah and in the diaspora after the exile, learning what it means to be God's people without a king, gathered around temple and Torah.
2138: Persian-period Jerusalem and Judah, from Cyrus' decree (538 BC) and the rebuilding of the temple (completed 516/515 BC) to Ezra's mission in the reign of Artaxerxes.
2139: To show God fulfilling the promise of return by moving the hearts of Persian kings, to record the rebuilding of the temple against opposition, and to describe Ezra's reforms re-establishing the community on the law.
2142: The law of Moses as the community's charter
2143: Holiness and separation, including the problem of intermarriage
2145: Cyrus' decree and the first return
2149: Haggai, Zechariah and completion of the temple
2154: Ezra shows the first return from exile and the rebuilding of the temple, a real but partial fulfilment of the prophets' promises of restoration. The modest second temple and the community's struggles leave readers looking for a greater restoration, which the Gospels announce in Jesus.
2155: Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew Bible and in early Christian lists; Origen and Jerome attest the division. Naming is confusing: the Vulgate calls Ezra '1 Esdras' and Nehemiah '2 Esdras'. A separate Greek book, *1 Esdras* (Vulgate '3 Esdras'), retells material from 2 Chr 35-36, Ezra and Neh 8 with an added story of three guardsmen; it is canonical in the Eastern Orthodox Church and appears in the Vulgate appendix and the Protestant Apocrypha. *2 Esdras* (also called 4 Ezra), a Jewish-Christian apocalypse, is in the Vulgate appendix, the Protestant Apocrypha and some Eastern canons (e.g. Ethiopian); it is not in the Catholic deuterocanon.
2158: Nehemiah wrote the first-person memoir; the Talmud credits Ezra with the book as a whole, with Nehemiah completing it (Baba Bathra 15a).
2159: Widely accepted that a genuine 'Nehemiah Memoir' (roughly Neh 1-7 and parts of Neh 12-13) underlies the book, with lists and the Ezra material of Neh 8-10 added by the compiler of Ezra–Nehemiah. The Elephantine papyri (late 5th c. BC) mention Sanballat as governor of Samaria and Johanan as high priest in Jerusalem, providing external corroboration of figures and setting.
2161: The struggling community in Jerusalem and Judah after the exile, and diaspora Jews concerned for the holy city.
2162: Susa and Jerusalem during the reign of Artaxerxes I; Nehemiah arrives as governor in his twentieth year (445 BC) and returns for a second term about twelve years later.
2163: To record how God used Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem's walls against opposition, to show the people recommitting to the law under Ezra, and to warn against slipping back into the sins that caused the exile.
2166: Public reading and understanding of Scripture
2178: Repopulation and dedication of the walls
2180: Nehemiah is the last narrative of Israel's history in the Hebrew Bible's timeline: the walls are rebuilt, yet the book ends with the people already falling back into old sins. That unresolved ending points to the need for a deeper renewal of hearts, which the prophets promised and the New Testament proclaims.
2181: Originally one book with Ezra in the Hebrew Bible; called '2 Esdras' in the Vulgate. In the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments the deuterocanonical books of *Tobit* and *Judith* follow Nehemiah (see the note on Esther).
2183: Narrative (court story; historical narrative or historical novella, debated)
2184: The Talmud credits the 'Men of the Great Assembly' with writing Esther (Baba Bathra 15a); some Jewish and Christian interpreters (e.g. Ibn Ezra) suggested Mordecai, citing Esth 9:20.
2185: Anonymous, by a Jewish writer familiar with Persian court life. Scholars debate genre and historicity: some read it as history set in the reign of Xerxes I (Ahasuerus, 486–465 BC), noting accurate details of Persian administration and the palace at Susa; others read it as a historical novella or festival legend explaining Purim, pointing to the absence of Esther and Vashti in Greek sources (Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris) and to its literary symmetry.
2186: Soon after the events, late Persian period
2188: Jews living in the diaspora under foreign rule, explaining the origin of Purim and assuring them of deliverance even when God seems absent.
2189: The Persian capital Susa during the reign of Ahasuerus (usually identified with Xerxes I), about 483–473 BC.
2190: To tell how the Jews were saved from Haman's genocidal plot through Esther and Mordecai, to establish the annual feast of Purim, and to show hidden providence at work through human courage and remarkable reversals.
2204: Deliverance and the feast of Purim
2206: Esther shows God preserving his people in exile, keeping alive the line through which his promises would be fulfilled, even when he works behind the scenes. Its story of a mediator who risks her life to intercede for a condemned people has often been read by Christians as foreshadowing Christ.
2207: In the Hebrew Bible Esther belongs to the Writings among the five Megillot and is read at Purim. It never names God and is the only Hebrew Bible book not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls; its canonicity was questioned by some rabbis and early Christians. The Greek version adds six passages (Additions A–F, about 107 verses), including Mordecai's dream, the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, and the texts of the royal edicts, which make God explicit; these are canonical in Catholic (deuterocanonical) and Orthodox Bibles, and Jerome gathered them at the end as Esth 10:4-16:24 in the Vulgate. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also place the deuterocanonical *Tobit* (a pious exile's family story set in Nineveh) and *Judith* (a widow who delivers Israel from Holofernes) next to Esther; Protestant Bibles that print them place them among the Apocrypha.
2209: Wisdom literature (poetic dialogue within a prose frame)
2210: Moses, according to one view in the Talmud (Baba Bathra 14b-15a); other ancient suggestions include Job himself, Elihu or Solomon. Its patriarchal setting led many to see it as very ancient.
2211: An anonymous Israelite poet of great skill, writing in Hebrew rich with rare vocabulary. Many scholars date the poetry between the 7th and 4th centuries BC, often around the exile, and compare it with Mesopotamian works on innocent suffering such as *Ludlul bel nemeqi* and the *Babylonian Theodicy*. Some regard the prose frame as an older folk tale and the Elihu speeches (Job 32-37) and wisdom poem (Job 28) as later additions; others defend the book's unity as a deliberate design.
2214: The faithful wrestling with suffering that seems undeserved, and wisdom teachers tempted to explain all suffering as punishment.
2215: The land of Uz (perhaps in Edom or northern Arabia) in a patriarchal-style world, with Job as a wealthy non-Israelite who fears God.
2216: To explore whether anyone serves God for nothing, to challenge a mechanical view that suffering always reflects sin, and to bring Job, and the reader, before the wisdom and freedom of God the Creator.
2218: The limits of human wisdom and retributive theology
2219: Honest lament and protest before God
2222: Prologue in heaven and on earth
2227: Job's final defence and oath of innocence
2229: The LORD answers from the whirlwind; Job responds
2231: Job wrestles with the question raised by the fall and by Israel's suffering: how can a good and powerful God allow the righteous to suffer? Its picture of a blameless sufferer and its longing for a redeemer and mediator (Job 9:33; Job 19:25) are taken up in Christian reflection on Christ, and James points to Job as a model of endurance (Jas 5:11).
2232: In the Hebrew Bible Job belongs to the Writings, alongside Psalms and Proverbs as one of the three 'poetic books' with a special accent system. The Old Greek translation is roughly one-sixth shorter than the Hebrew; Origen filled the gaps from Theodotion's version. The Greek also adds a closing note identifying Job with Jobab king of Edom (compare Gen 36:33).
2234: Poetry (hymns, laments, thanksgivings, royal and wisdom psalms)
2235: David as the principal author: 73 psalms carry the Hebrew heading 'of David', and the New Testament cites several as David's words (e.g. Acts 2:25-31 on Ps 16). Other headings name Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon (Ps 72; Ps 127), Moses (Ps 90), Heman and Ethan; about fifty psalms have no named author.
2236: Most critical scholars treat the psalm headings as later additions and note that Hebrew *ledavid* can mean 'of', 'for' or 'belonging to' David. Hermann Gunkel's form criticism classified psalms by type and setting in worship; more recent 'canonical' study (e.g. Gerald Wilson) examines the shaping of the five-book collection. Individual psalms range from the monarchy (or earlier) to the post-exilic period (Ps 137 reflects the exile), with the collection reaching its final form in the Persian or early Hellenistic era.
2240: Israel at worship, both in the temple and in private prayer; later the synagogue and the church, which adopted the Psalms as their primary prayer book.
2241: Composed across many centuries, from David's court and the Jerusalem temple to the Babylonian exile and the second temple.
2242: To give God's people words for praise, lament, confession, thanksgiving and trust, to celebrate the LORD's kingship and his anointed king, and to train them in meditation on God's instruction.
2250: Introduction: the two ways and the LORD's anointed
2252: Book II: Korah and David psalms
2253: Book III: Asaph psalms; crisis of the Davidic covenant
2254: Book IV: Moses' prayer and the LORD reigns
2259: The Psalms are Israel's response to the whole story of God's acts: creation, exodus, kingship, exile and hope of restoration. They are the Old Testament book most quoted in the New Testament; Jesus prays Ps 22 and Ps 31 on the cross and identifies himself with the Lord of Ps 110, and the church has sung them ever since.
2260: The Psalms open the Writings in most Hebrew Bible orderings. The Septuagint and Vulgate number most psalms one lower than the Hebrew because they join Ps 9-10 and Ps 114-115 and split Ps 116 and Ps 147; older Catholic and Orthodox liturgical books follow this Greek numbering. The Septuagint adds *Psalm 151*, about David's victory over Goliath, which is canonical in Orthodox Bibles; a Hebrew form of it was found in the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a), whose order and contents differ from the Masoretic book in its final third.
2262: Wisdom literature (instructions and collections of sayings)
2263: Solomon as principal author (Prov 1:1; Prov 10:1; compare 1 Kgs 4:32), with other sections attributed to 'the wise', to Hezekiah's scribes who copied Solomonic proverbs (Prov 25:1), to Agur (Prov 30) and to King Lemuel (Prov 31). The Talmud credits Hezekiah and his company with writing it down (Baba Bathra 15a).
2264: An anthology of several collections assembled over centuries. Many accept that some sayings go back to the royal court of the monarchy, and Prov 22:17-24:22 closely parallels the Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope*, showing Israel's engagement with international wisdom. Prov 1-9 is often thought to be the latest section, composed as an introduction in the Persian period, though some argue for earlier dates based on ancient Near Eastern instruction forms.
2266: Final edition with Prov 1-9 as introduction
2267: Young people being trained for responsible life ('my son'), and by extension anyone seeking skill in living under God.
2268: Royal court, scribal schools and family instruction in Israel and Judah, drawing also on wider ancient Near Eastern wisdom.
2269: To teach wisdom, discipline and right conduct grounded in the fear of the LORD, contrasting the way of wisdom with the way of folly in speech, work, wealth, family and justice.
2270: The fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom
2271: Wisdom personified as a woman calling in the streets
2274: Justice and care for the poor
2275: Prologue and a father's instructions; Lady Wisdom and Folly
2278: Solomonic proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
2281: A mother's advice to a king
2283: Proverbs shows what covenant faithfulness looks like in everyday life, rooting practical skill in reverence for God the Creator. Its portrait of Wisdom present with God at creation (Prov 8) shaped New Testament language about Christ as the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24; Col 2:3) and the Word in John 1.
